passage: Damini opened the maths notebook and stared. In Coimbatore her class had done fractions last term, but here the children were already on ratios. At lunch the Hindi flew past too fast, and when she answered, two girls giggled at how she stretched her words. She carried her tiffin to the corner of the bench. Aditi, who sat in the row ahead, turned around. "Want me to show you how Ma'am does ratios? I'll do it at recess." Damini nodded, her throat tight. That evening Mummy set out the same routine as always: warm milk, one chapter of a storybook, lights off at nine. Damini told her about Aditi, and slept easily.

qa.q: Where had Damini's class already done fractions last term?
qa.a: In Coimbatore, her class had done fractions last term.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when two girls giggled at how she stretched her words?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and out of place, which is why she took her tiffin to the corner of the bench.

qa.q: What made the biggest difference to Damini's day, and what steadied her at home?
qa.a: Aditi's offer to explain ratios at recess turned the day around, and Mummy's usual routine of warm milk, a chapter and lights off at nine steadied her at home.

qa.q: Why might Aditi have turned around to speak to Damini?
qa.a: Aditi may have noticed Damini sitting alone in the corner and struggling with the maths, and wanted to help. 🙂

grounding: A child changing schools after a move struggles with accent and syllabus, and a kind classmate and a steady home routine help.

passage:
"You're sitting alone again," said Raghav, dropping his bag on the bench.
"I'm fine." Joseph pushed his rice around. "They laugh at how I say my words."
"Riya laughs at everything. She laughed at my glasses on the first day." Raghav grinned. "Which chapter are you stuck on?"
"All of it. In Kochi we did the water cycle last year. Here it's already the human body."
"Come to my desk. My brother's old notes are really neat."
"Really?"
"Really. And say that word again, I like it."
Joseph laughed for the first time all week. "Amma says I can call Kochi on Sunday evening if I keep my homework hour every day."
"Then keep it," said Raghav. "I'll save you a seat tomorrow."

qa.q: From which city had Joseph come?
What was Joseph feeling when he said the other children laugh at how he says his words?
qa.a: He felt hurt and alone, which shows in how he pushed his rice around and sat by himself.

qa.q: What could Joseph do next to feel settled in the new school?
qa.a: He could go to Raghav's desk to use the neat notes and keep his daily homework hour, which Amma links to his Sunday call to Kochi.

qa.q: Why might Raghav be quick to notice Joseph sitting alone?
qa.a: Raghav mentions that Riya laughed at his glasses on the first day, so he seems to know how being laughed at feels. 🙂

grounding: A child who changed schools after a move struggles with accent and syllabus, and a kind classmate and home routine help.
